transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

I guess… work is what pushed me to come in. I’m an industrial production manager, and I got into this mode where I was launching plant redesign projects nonstop, calling suppliers after hours, rewriting the shift plan all by myself—like I could somehow fix the whole place if I just kept going.

And then it kind of flipped. Suddenly I couldn’t keep up with all the plans I’d set in motion. There were just too many moving pieces, and I was the one who started them. It’s embarrassing, honestly. I’m usually pretty good at keeping things controlled.
Have you been feeling overly anxious or worried about things other than work lately?

I don’t know… I mean, work is the big thing I keep circling back to. Other stuff, maybe, but it all kind of gets tangled together. Like if I’m worried about my apartment being messy, it turns into thinking about whether I’m organized enough in general, and then somehow I’m back to the plant schedule again.

So… I’m not sure I’d say it’s other things, exactly. It’s hard for me to separate it out.
Do you often feel guilty about things?

Guilty… I don’t know. I mean, I feel bad when things slip, especially if someone else has to pick up the pieces. But “guilty” makes it sound like I did something wrong on purpose, and I don’t think that’s exactly it.

Sometimes I replay conversations, like with supervisors or my team, and wonder if I came off too harsh or made things harder. But then I’ll start thinking about the whole production line and staffing and whether the redesign timeline was even realistic, and… sorry, I’m kind of drifting. I’m not sure if it’s guilt or just feeling responsible for everything.
Do you often feel worthless or like you're not good enough?

I’m not sure. “Worthless” feels like a really big word, and I don’t know if I’d say that. Not good enough… maybe sometimes, but then I start comparing it to, like, performance reviews or whether I met the production targets, and that’s not exactly the same thing, is it?

I guess I have moments where I wonder if I’m falling short, but I don’t know if that’s what you mean. It kind of depends on the day, and on what just happened.
Do you often feel like you're not good enough outside of work?

Outside of work… I’m not sure, honestly. I think I don’t separate it very well. Like if my apartment is a mess, I’ll start thinking, okay, is this just because I was busy, or does this mean I’m bad at being an adult, you know? But then my brain kind of drags it back to work anyway.

So I don’t know if I feel “not good enough” outside of work on its own. It’s more like everything gets measured against whether I’m keeping things together, and work is usually the thing I use to measure that.
Do you often feel like you're just pretending to be competent?

Pretending… I’m not sure. I mean, sometimes I feel like I’m piecing things together as I go, but I don’t know if that’s pretending or just how everyone works.

Like, at work there are so many moving parts—machines, schedules, people calling out, supervisors needing answers—and half the time you’re making decisions with incomplete information anyway. So if I seem competent, maybe it’s because I’m good at organizing chaos, or maybe it’s just because I’ve learned the right tone to use in meetings. I don’t know.

Outside of that… I guess I haven’t really thought of it as pretending. More like trying not to let people see when I’m unsure. But isn’t that kind of normal?
Have you had any days where you couldn't do your usual work or activities because of how you were feeling?

Yeah… there have been a couple days like that. I mean, I try not to call out or make it a big thing, because once you’re the person who’s supposed to be keeping the line moving, it’s hard to admit you’re the bottleneck.

There was one day where I had to ask to be pulled out of a shift-planning meeting. I just couldn’t… make the basic calls I’m supposed to make, like staffing decisions and production priorities. And those meetings are usually boring but manageable, you know, like everyone arguing about coverage and whether maintenance actually finished what they said they finished—

But that time I couldn’t carry out the normal decisions my role depends on. Occupational health ended up getting involved, which felt humiliating, honestly. I kept thinking, if I can’t do that part, then what am I even doing there?
Do you often feel nervous or anxious around other people, outside of work?

I’m not sure I’d call it nervous, exactly. Outside of work I don’t… I don’t have a neat category for it.

Like, if I’m at a friend’s thing or with family, I’m usually more thinking about whether I’m being normal, or whether I should’ve brought something, or if I’m staying too long—actually, that reminds me, my aunt has this whole thing about people not taking leftovers, which somehow turns into a comment on your manners, and then I’m thinking about that instead of the conversation.

But anxious around people? I don’t know. Maybe sometimes, but I haven’t really tracked it that way. What do you mean by anxious—like panicky, or just uncomfortable?
Do you often feel anxious or on edge even when there's no obvious reason to be?

I don’t know… “no obvious reason” is the part I get stuck on, because usually I can find a reason if I look hard enough. Like, there’s always something—some email I forgot, some weird tone someone used, the fact that my apartment has that one corner where mail just sort of becomes archaeology.

But anxious or on edge just out of nowhere? I haven’t really noticed it that cleanly. Sometimes I’ll feel keyed up, but then I’ll start tracing it back and think, well, maybe it was the meeting earlier, or the noise from the upstairs neighbor, or I didn’t eat properly. So I’m not sure if that counts.

What do you mean by on edge—like physically tense, or more like worrying?
Do you often feel anxious for no specific reason that you can identify?

I mean… I don’t really know. I keep trying to answer that, but “no specific reason” is hard for me because if I sit with it long enough, I can usually attach it to something.

Like yesterday I felt kind of wound up, but then I was thinking, well, maybe it was because I hadn’t replied to my cousin, or because the grocery delivery substituted the wrong coffee creamer—which sounds stupid, but then it changes your whole morning, and then you’re late, and then you’re annoyed before anything even happens.

So… I haven’t noticed it as just anxiety floating there with no reason. Or maybe I’m bad at telling when there isn’t a reason.
Do you often find yourself worrying about things even when everything seems to be going well?

I’m not sure. I mean, “everything going well” is kind of… slippery, because even when things look fine, I can usually think of something that could go wrong. Like if work is fine and my apartment is mostly clean and nobody’s mad at me, then I’ll remember I haven’t checked my tire pressure in forever, or that one bill that’s probably on autopay but what if it isn’t.

But I don’t know if I’d call that worrying, exactly, or just… keeping track of life? My mom used to make these lists on the fridge, and she’d put even tiny things on there, like “buy foil,” and somehow that made it feel like the whole house depended on foil. Sorry, that’s not really the question.

So, do I worry when things are going well? Maybe sometimes, but I haven’t really noticed it as a pattern.
Do you often find yourself worrying about things for a long time after they've happened?

I’m not totally sure. I mean, I’ll think back on things after they happen, but I don’t know if it’s “worrying for a long time” or just replaying it because my brain wants the file organized properly, if that makes sense.

Like if I said something weird in a meeting, I might remember it later while I’m washing a pan or trying to find my keys, but then I’ll also be thinking about the pan, and how my old roommate used to burn eggs in this one skillet and somehow it always smelled like pennies—sorry, that’s not related.

So… I don’t know. I haven’t really tracked how long it lasts. What counts as a long time?
Do you often find yourself worrying about the future?

I don’t know… I mean, the future is such a big category. Like, do you mean big future, like where I’ll be in five years, or smaller future, like whether I’m going to forget to take the laundry out before it smells weird?

Because I think about upcoming stuff, sure, but I don’t always know if that’s “worrying” or just planning. At work, if we don’t think ahead, things go sideways fast, so my brain sort of stays in that mode. Even at home I’ll be like, okay, if I don’t buy dish soap today then tomorrow morning is going to be annoying, and then I’m thinking about the store layout because they moved the cleaning aisle last month for no reason.

So… I guess I haven’t really noticed whether I often worry about the future specifically. I’d need to pay more attention to that.
Do you often find yourself worrying about things even when there's nothing in particular that's causing you stress?

I’m not sure how to separate “nothing in particular” from, like… the general background noise of life. Because even if there isn’t one obvious stress thing, there’s still always something, right? Groceries, work emails, whether I answered someone too bluntly, the weird clicking sound my fridge makes—though that might actually be normal, I looked it up once and then got stuck reading about compressor cycles for way too long.

But, um… if you mean do I just sit there worried when nothing is really happening, I don’t know. I haven’t noticed it clearly. Sometimes my mind is busy, but I’m not sure I’d label it as worrying.
Do you often find yourself worrying about everyday things, like chores or minor tasks, even when they are not necessarily problematic?

I’m not really sure. Everyday things do kind of float around in my head, like chores and errands, but I don’t always know if I’d call it worrying.

Like dishes, for example—if there are dishes in the sink, I’ll think about them, but then I’m also thinking about whether the sponge smells weird, and then I remember I meant to buy a new sponge, and then somehow I’m thinking about how the grocery store lighting makes all the produce look fake. So it’s not always, like, “Oh no, this is a problem,” it’s more that my brain keeps touching the topic.

I guess I haven’t paid attention to whether it happens even when the task isn’t actually problematic. It’s kind of hard for me to separate that out.
Do you often find yourself preoccupied with thoughts about everyday tasks or responsibilities, even when they are not urgent or important?

I’m not totally sure. I mean, I do think about tasks when they’re not urgent, but sometimes it’s just because they’re in my line of sight. Like if I see the mail pile, then I remember the one envelope that might be important, except half the time it’s just some insurance thing written in that tiny font nobody actually wants to read.

But “preoccupied” sounds like… stuck on it? I don’t know if I get stuck exactly. My mind jumps around responsibilities a lot, especially if I’m moving through the apartment and every room has, like, a different reminder in it. But I haven’t really tracked whether those things are important or not. It’s just kind of… there.
Do you often find yourself worrying about things like chores, tasks, or daily responsibilities even when they are not pressing or out of the ordinary?

I don’t really know. I keep circling that word “worrying,” because if I’m thinking about laundry at 11 p.m., is that worry or just… laundry existing in my brain?

Sometimes I’ll notice small responsibilities kind of stacking up in my head, like emails or groceries or whether I forgot to move something at work, but then my mind veers off into some random detail, like the exact aisle where they moved the cereal, and I lose the thread. So I can’t honestly say I’ve noticed a clear pattern of worrying when things aren’t pressing.

It’s more like mental clutter, maybe? I’m not sure if that’s what you mean.
Do you often find yourself worrying about things for more than a few days at a time?

I’m not sure. More than a few days… I guess some things do come back around, but I don’t know if I’d call it worrying the whole time.

Like I might think about an email I haven’t answered on Monday, then forget it, then remember it again Wednesday because I see the little unread number, and then I’m annoyed at the unread number itself because it’s like this tiny red accusation. But that’s not exactly me sitting there worried for three days straight.

So… I don’t know. I haven’t really noticed whether it lasts that long in a clear way.
Do you feel like your worrying or anxiety has been affecting your daily life for a long time?

I’m not sure, honestly. “For a long time” is hard for me to measure, because daily life always has so many moving parts. Like at work there’s always some production schedule or supply issue or someone asking about a spreadsheet, and then at home it’s dishes or messages or—sorry, that’s probably not what you mean.

I guess I haven’t really noticed whether anxiety itself has been affecting things over a long stretch. Sometimes I feel like I’m just reacting to whatever is in front of me, and then later I can’t tell if it was worry or just normal life being noisy. So… I don’t know how to answer that clearly.
Have you been feeling anxious or worried for most of the past six months?

I don’t know if I can say “most” of six months. Six months is such a weird block of time to hold in my head—like I can remember specific weeks better than the whole stretch. 

I’ve had anxious moments, I think, but then I start sorting them by what was actually happening at work or at home, and then it turns into this whole mental filing cabinet thing. Like was I worried because something needed doing, or was I just thinking about it because it was there? I’m not sure.

So… I haven’t really noticed it clearly enough to say yes, I’ve been anxious or worried most of that time.
